title: Fifteen thousand year old clay birds point to an earlier symbolic tradition
dek: Researchers re-examined heated clay from three Natufian settlements and identified 154 figurative artefacts, including birds, animals and human forms, dating to a time before agriculture.
body: The clay pieces come from el-Wad Terrace on Mount Carmel, Hayonim Terrace in Galilee, and Eynan-Mallaha in the Upper Jordan Valley. The study reports that they date to the Natufian culture, which flourished between approximately 15,000 and 11,650 years ago. These hunter-fisher-gatherer communities were adopting increasingly sedentary lifestyles before fully agricultural societies appeared in the Neolithic.

Researchers re-examined collections containing tens of thousands of small pieces of heated clay and sediment from the three settlements. Those pieces had previously been associated largely with the production of mineral pigments. The team identified 15 figurines and 139 cylindrical fragments interpreted as probable fragments of figurative objects, including body parts and appendages.

Eleven of the 15 figurines represent birds. Some appear to show waterfowl such as ducks, geese or swans, while others may depict birds of prey. Several were modelled with cylindrical necks and downward-facing heads, a posture researchers suggest could represent courtship displays observed among waterfowl.

Two fragments may represent hoofed animals, including one that could depict a mountain gazelle. Small impressions in the clay suggest perishable materials, possibly twigs, were inserted to represent horns or antlers. If this interpretation is correct, the artefact would be among the earliest known composite figurines from Southwest Asia, combining clay with perishable materials.

One figurine depicts the upper part of a human body with modelled arms, while another represents a stylised face that may have carried decorations made from grasses, fibres, hair or feathers. Microscopic examination revealed fingerprints, palm impressions and fingertip depressions, along with marks from shaping, smoothing, grooving and incision.

Ten of the eleven bird figurines have traces of red colouring. One Early Natufian example was coated with an iron-rich clay slip, and the study says this is the earliest evidence known for use of an engobe colouring technique. All of the clay objects had been heated, but researchers do not know whether they were fired intentionally, passively heated near fires or accidentally burned after deposition.

Fingerprints and manufacturing traces show that children as well as adults made clay objects, offering insight into the demographics of craft production in Natufian communities. Prior to this study only two clay figurines had been identified in the Natufian record, and figurative use of clay in Southwest Asia was generally associated with later Neolithic societies.

The newly identified assemblage puts the development of a mature clay figurative tradition much earlier, among hunter-gatherer communities transitioning towards sedentary life. Researchers say the findings push part of Southwest Asia's so-called revolution of symbols back into Epipalaeolithic times, showing developments in symbolic expression and clay technology were already happening before agriculture emerged.
doesnt_show: The study does not show the meaning or function of the figurines, nor does it establish whether the heated clay was fired intentionally or burned accidentally after deposition.
settle: Further analysis of the heating histories and exposure temperatures would clarify how the objects were treated and whether they were deliberately fired.
